scam_lead: If money or an account is compromised, act immediately. Note the time and reference number at every step.
scam_note: This is first-step guidance, not legal advice. Always check NCCIA or bank numbers against an official source; the emergency directory only lists admin-verified numbers.
scam_step_1: Stop contact with the fraudster and do not send more money.
scam_step_2: Call your bank or wallet provider immediately and ask to block or freeze the card/account.
scam_step_3: Change your bank, email and social-media passwords; turn on two-step verification where available.
scam_step_4: Preserve evidence: screenshots, transaction IDs, messages, call logs and the website link.
scam_step_5: Write down the date, time, amount, IBAN/wallet number and the fraudster's ID.
scam_step_6: File a written complaint with your bank's fraud desk and get a complaint number.
scam_step_7: Report to NCCIA (cyber crime) through its official complaint portal or helpline; keep the ticket number.
scam_step_8: If money went through a wallet, agent or online platform, also write to that provider.
scam_step_9: If someone impersonated a bank or government office, tell the real institution and get an incident reference.
scam_step_10: Check your email, SIM and bank alerts; report any new login or SIM change immediately.
scam_step_11: Avoid people who demand an advance fee to 'recover' your money; that can be a second scam.
scam_step_12: Never share an OTP, PIN, password or CNIC, even if the caller claims to be from a bank, police or government office.
scam_step_13: If your CNIC or documents were exposed, monitor their use and notify the relevant authority in writing.
scam_step_14: Keep following up with the bank and NCCIA; save every reference number and reply.
scam_step_15: For free first-step legal help, write a request on Insaf Dastak or contact a verified helpline.
